guide.intro: Google DSA roadmap, research-updated Sept 2026. For 5–6 focused hours/day, first interviews month 3–4, ~3–4/10 on unseen mediums. Built from LeetCode Discuss candidate reports (2024–2026), topic-frequency analysis across ~600 reported Google problems, and Google's 2026 process changes. ~200 new problems on purpose — candidates who cleared report 150–250 with deep understanding, not 500+ shallow.

research.title: There's a gate before the interviews: the GHA
research.text: The Google Hiring Assessment is a pass/fail behavioural screen that arrives 24–72 h after applying — 50–75 Likert statements, 30 minutes, one sitting, no back button, ~4–5 day deadline, reported six-month reapply window. It measures integrity, collaboration, ownership, ambiguity-handling and communication, and cross-checks consistency. Handle it in week 0.

research.title: Google problems come wrapped in ambiguity
research.text: The most consistent 2025–2026 theme isn't difficulty — it's deliberately vague framing. "Parse a chat log and return the K most talkative users", "a network of teleporters, some broken, return the path". Underneath: top-K heap, BFS, DP. The algorithm is standard; the statement is not. Nobody practises this, and it's why strong LeetCode solvers fail Google specifically.

research.title: The 2026 process has changed
research.text: In-person rounds are back at many locations. AI is banned in standard loops (policy varies by round — confirm with your recruiter). A code-comprehension round is piloting (read and debug an unfamiliar 200–500 line codebase in CoderPad). L3 has no system design round; L4 sometimes chooses three coding rounds.

research.title: Topic frequency decides where hours go
research.text: Arrays + Trees + DP + Graphs ≈ 63% of ~600 reported problems; those four are weeks 1–9. Google has the highest hard share in FAANG (~19%), and graph problems are displacing pure string problems in 2026 OA rounds.

research.title: On the Premium Google tag
research.text: Contested value. Use the Discuss interview-experience compilations instead — one L3 offer-holder compiled every Google question from 2022–2024 posts and hit three verbatim in his loop. If you buy Premium, one month for weeks 9–14 only.

rules: No editorial before 25 minutes. Not a hint, not a tag, not an LLM.
Every problem is re-solved at +3 and +14 days, from a blank file. This converts exposure into retrieval and is the direct fix for 3–4/10.
After the editorial: close it, re-implement from scratch.
Tagged practice is fine in Phase 1. Untagged from Phase 2, except the weekly measurement set which is untagged from week 1.
20% of all practice happens in a blank Google Doc or on paper. No IDE, no autocomplete, no execution. With in-person rounds back, add whiteboard or paper sessions from week 9.

dailyTemplate.content: 3 new problems (2 on hard days and all of weeks 6–7). 25-min hard timer → 5 min writing what you know and which constraint you haven't used → editorial → close → re-implement blank.
The day's +3 and +14 queue. Even on bad days. Short on time? Cut Block A, never Block B.
Editorials incl. alternate approaches · trigger notes · triage drill (15 min) · one variant, mandatory.
Blind primitives — pick 5 (daily, 20 min) + rotation: Tue debug hunt · Wed code quality · Thu ambiguity drill · Fri code comprehension · Sat cold-combo.

dailyNotes: Weekly shape: 5 full days + 1 contest half-day + 1 full rest day.
Contest day (3h): 90-min LeetCode weekly or biweekly, 90-min post-mortem solving everything missed, untimed. Then stop.

phase2Template.content: 2 problems, random and untagged, 40/60 medium/hard, spoken aloud, recorded, 2 variants each, half of them posed as ambiguous scenarios.

drills.name: Spaced re-solve
drills.text: 12-minute timebox. Can't finish → failure → re-queue +3/+14 from today. Clean pass at +14 → retire. Failed twice → add +30. Passing means you reconstructed the reasoning, not recalled the code — typed something memorised and can't state the invariant out loud? Fail, even if it submits green.

drills.name: Ambiguity drill
drills.text: Take a solved problem and rewrite it as a vague real-world scenario the way a Google interviewer would pose it. Come back to it a week later (or have a friend read it cold) and practise the derivation out loud: clarifying questions, stated assumptions, explicit edge cases. Source scenarios from Discuss Google interview-experience posts.

drills.name: Variant generation
drills.text: After solving anything, pick one variant and solve it. Reported Google rounds routinely include 2–3 follow-ups after the initial solve — this drill is the second half of every round.

drills.name: Triage
drills.text: Ten problems you will not solve, 90 seconds each: constraints suggest · trigger phrase · pattern guess · why not greedy. Then check tags. Ten pattern-recognition reps at a tenth the cost of solving ten.

drills.name: Blind primitives
drills.text: 2 you failed most recently (from the bug log) · 2 you haven't touched in a week · 1 from this week's topic. Instantiate, don't stub. Verify every attempt by pasting into a real problem. Retire nothing, but taper: clean four times running → monthly spot-check.

drills.name: Debug hunt
drills.text: Break a solved problem deliberately (off-by-one, flipped comparison, missing base case, answer recorded before the shrink). Wait a day. Find it by hand-tracing a small input — no execution. Exactly what a shared-doc round demands.

drills.name: Code quality pass
drills.text: Rewrite two of the week's solutions as if for code review: descriptive names, extracted helpers, guard clauses, no magic numbers. Could an interviewer follow this while you narrate? Google grades readability explicitly.

drills.name: Code comprehension
drills.text: Open an unfamiliar 200–500 line file from a real open-source repo, ideally a language you don't write daily. Out loud: what does it do in two sentences · inputs, outputs, invariants · where would a bug hide · complexity of the hot path · what would you change. This is the pilot round's exact shape.

drills.name: Cold-combo
drills.text: Write a primitive inside an actual problem under time pressure, rather than in isolation. The check against a skeleton becoming its own memorised artifact.

guide.bugLog: Every failed primitive attempt gets one line, e.g. "Dijkstra — forgot to skip stale PQ entries on pop". This selects your first two primitives each day; after a month it maps your personal bug fingerprint. Keep it in Notes.

guide.primitivesGoal: Blank file, zero reference, timed. 22 primitives; targets are fluency targets, not learning targets. Daily: pick 5 — 2 you failed most recently, 2 untouched for a week, 1 from this week's topic. #9, #18 and #21 carry path reconstruction deliberately: "return the actual sequence, not the value" is one of Google's most common follow-ups.

Return the actual sequence/path, not just its length/value

trigger phrase: "minimum number of X such that..."

verbalProtocol: Restate the problem in your own words. Confirm.

Ask 2–3 clarifying questions and state your assumptions explicitly — with Google's ambiguous framing this is scored. Input size? Duplicates? Ties? Who parses the input? Fits in memory? Return the value or the actual path?
State a brute force and its complexity. Skipping this reads as pattern-matching.
Propose the optimisation and its complexity before coding.
Code, narrating. Clean names — readability is graded.
Dry-run a small example by hand, out loud. No execution available.
Volunteer your own test cases — interviewers ask candidates to enumerate test scenarios unprompted.
State time and space complexity, justified. Offer a follow-up improvement.
googleyness: Disagreeing with a senior engineer's technical decision (reported 2026 prompt)
A project you drove without authority
exitCriteria: Unseen medium: pattern in ≤5 min, solved in ≤25, bug-free first submission, ~80% of the time.
Unseen hard: solved in 40–45 min about half the time.
Ambiguous scenario → correct specification in ≤5 min of clarifying questions.
Two follow-up variants handled on the spot without restarting.
From memory in under 8 min: Dijkstra · Union-Find · both topological sorts · LIS O(n log n) · trie · quickselect · two-heaps median · edit distance grid.
New DP problem: state / transition / base / order correct before any code.
Time and space stated and justified unprompted, every time.
Ten Googleyness stories written and rehearsed; GHA completed.
failureModes: Failing the GHA before you ever code. Handle it in week 0.
Skipping Block B. Revision feels unproductive because you're re-solving things you "already know." You don't.
Practising only clean problem statements. Google's ambiguity is intentional; the Thursday drill exists for this.
Skipping variants. At Google that's skipping half of every round.
Jumping straight to optimal. Reads as memorisation. State the brute force.
Practising only mediums. Google has the highest hard share in FAANG.
Only practising in an IDE. Shared doc, no autocomplete, no execution — and in-person rounds mean paper too.
Skipping the rest day. A burnout crash costs two weeks you don't have.
recruiter: In-person or remote? Determines paper vs shared-doc practice.
Does my loop include the code-comprehension round? If yes, weight the Friday drill heavily.
Is AI permitted in any round? Policy is per-round now. Assume banned unless you have it in writing.

guide.scope: L3 has no system design round. L4 sometimes chooses three coding rounds over two coding + one design. Targeting L3/L4, the only non-DSA prep is the GHA and the Googleyness round. L5+ needs a separate system design track. Process details reflect reporting as of September 2026 — re-check before your loop.

weeks.title: Week 0 — GHA & diagnostic

items.name: Read Google's published values and the "Googleyness" language
Write your genuine positions: owning a mistake under pressure · disagreeing with a senior engineer · ambiguous requirements · sharing credit · escalating vs resolving · handling sensitive data
Decide: answer decisively and consistently, as yourself. Block a quiet 60 min when the invite arrives — no pause, no back button

Classify each failure: didn't see the pattern → triage 15/day · saw it, couldn't code → primitives daily · bugs → weekly debug hunt + dry-run habit · too slow → tighter timers, both contests
Record the score in Notes — weeks 4, 8 and 11 measure against it

notes: The GHA is a pass/fail behavioural screen that arrives 24–72 h after applying: 50–75 Likert statements, 30 minutes, one sitting, ~4–5 day deadline, reported six-month reapply window. You could do 400 hours of DSA and never reach a coding round. Handle it now.
It rewards defensible, decisive choices and cross-checks consistency across rephrased items. Answer as yourself, consistently — not as an imagined ideal candidate.

notes: Flagged problems are verified high-frequency in Google reports. Max Path Sum and Validate BST both appear repeatedly; Max Path Sum was identified as the basis of an actual Google India OA problem.

The pattern that matters most: post-order aggregate — recurse into children, get a tuple from each, combine at the node, return a possibly-different tuple upward while updating a global. Diameter, Max Path Sum, Balanced, House Robber III and Longest Univalue Path are the same algorithm in different clothes.
The recurring subtlety: what you return upward is often not what you record as the answer.
Block D aligned slot this week: post-order tree shell and iterative inorder.

notes: DP is 15% of reported problems and the only topic classified Hard across the board. Two weeks, two problems a day, done properly.

Non-negotiable format before any code: state (dp[i] = precise English meaning) · transition · base · order. Then recursive + memo → tabulation → space optimisation. Full chain on the first problem of each new sub-pattern only.
Coin Change vs Coin Change II differ only in loop order, and that difference is combinations vs permutations.
On LIS: also write the reconstruction. Returning the subsequence rather than its length is a standard follow-up.

systemDesign.budget: 1 hour a day, Monday to Saturday. Sunday is the rest day, as in the DSA plan.
systemDesign.intro: Concept-first system design: 33 concepts to master in eight weeks, one per day, each learned, written up as a card and tested with three interviewer probes; two design questions a week from week 1; then three weeks of recorded mocks scored with a rubric. Separate from the DSA plan — own schedule, own progress.

sessionShapes.shape: 10 min recall yesterday's card aloud with its probes · 35 min learn from the listed source, pen in hand (mechanism → what it buys → what it costs) · 15 min write the card from memory and answer the three probes aloud, then save the card in the concept's note.

5 min requirements and scope · 5 min numbers · 30 min design aloud on paper or a blank doc: API, data model, diagram, one deep dive · 15 min compare with the reference, list every missed concept and hand-waved number · 5 min post-mortem in the question's note.
45 min full interview format, aloud, recorded, interviewer-style follow-ups from the question's focus list · 15 min watch back and score with the rubric; write the score and the one fix in the note.
Cards only, no sources. Probes aloud, 60–90 s each. Anything not instant is rewritten from memory.

cardTemplate: What it is — two lines, as if explaining to a strong junior.
When to use it and when not to — one line each.
Mechanism → what it buys → what it costs — one line per mechanism.
Two failure modes an interviewer will probe, with the fix for each.
One real system that uses it and the choice it made.
The three probes, answered in one line each.
framework: Functional requirements (3 min): the three core features, explicit out-of-scope, confirm with the interviewer.
Non-functional requirements (3 min): scale (DAU, read/write QPS, data size, growth), latency per path, consistency vs availability per feature, durability, cost.
Back-of-envelope (4 min): QPS average and peak, storage per year, bandwidth, cache size. Say the numbers out loud and use them later to justify choices.
API (3 min): 3–5 endpoints with inputs, outputs, idempotency and pagination where relevant.
Data model (4 min): entities and access patterns, which store for which data and why, the partition key.
High-level diagram (8 min): client → DNS/CDN → load balancer → stateless services → cache → database → queue/log → workers. Draw it, then walk one read and one write through it.
Deep dives (15 min): the two hardest problems — hot keys, fan-out, consistency, idempotency, ordering, failover. Choose them yourself before being asked.
Scaling and failure (3 min): replication, partitioning, caching; what happens when each box dies; coordination only where unavoidable.
Trade-offs and wrap-up (2 min): what you gave up and why, what breaks at 10×, the first thing you'd change, what you'd monitor.
rubric: Problem navigation (1–4): clarified scope, chose the right three features, derived numbers and used them. 4 = drove the agenda without prompting.
Design (1–4): coherent high-level design, correct data model and store choices with reasons, clean API. 4 = every box justified by a requirement.
Depth (1–4): deep dives on the genuinely hard parts with concrete mechanisms, not 'add a cache'. 4 = named the failure modes and the fix for each.
Scaling and trade-offs (1–4): bottlenecks found, replication/partitioning/caching applied correctly, consistency choices explicit. 4 = explained what was given up.
Communication (1–4): structured, aloud, legible diagram, checked in, handled pushback by reasoning. 4 = the interviewer could present the design back.
Score every mock; a 4 everywhere on an unseen prompt is the goal. Any axis at 2 names the next recall drill.
googleRound: 45 minutes, open-ended, often vaguely phrased: a Google-scale product or data problem. Clarifying is scored — start there.
Interviewers drive deep dives on whatever you claim; every box you draw is a question you invited. Draw only what you can defend, then defend it with a number.
Reported prompts are data-heavy: timelines, autocomplete, view counts, photo storage, maps, metrics, logs, ad counting. Concepts 10–12, 20–23 and 30–31 are the vocabulary.
Level signal: L4 can be guided to a good design; L5 chooses the deep dives, states trade-offs unprompted and knows what to monitor. Practise the L5 behaviour regardless of target level.
Expect follow-ups on failure: what if this node dies, this region goes, this queue backs up, two users write at once. Answer with a mechanism and its cost, never 'it would be fine'.
Ask your recruiter whether your loop has a design round and whether it is whiteboard or shared doc; practise in that medium from week 9.
numbers: L1 cache 1 ns · main memory 100 ns · SSD random read 100 µs · HDD seek 10 ms
Round trip: same datacentre 0.5 ms · cross-continent 150 ms
Read 1 MB sequentially: memory 10 µs · SSD 1 ms · 1 Gbps network 10 ms · HDD 20 ms
1 day ≈ 86 400 s ≈ 10⁵ s · 1 M requests/day ≈ 12 QPS · 100 M DAU × 10 requests ≈ 12 k QPS average, plan for 2–3× peak
Sizes: char 1 B · UUID 16 B · tweet-like row 1 KB · photo 1 MB · 1 M × 1 KB = 1 GB · 1 B × 1 KB = 1 TB
One relational node: a few thousand writes/s, ~10 k simple reads/s · Redis ~100 k ops/s · one Kafka partition tens of MB/s · ~10 k open WebSockets per server. Order of magnitude is what matters.
exitCriteria: All 33 concept cards written from memory; any card's three probes answered instantly, aloud.
Unseen 45-minute prompt: requirements and numbers in ≤8 min, diagram by minute 20, two self-chosen deep dives with explicit trade-offs; rubric 4 on every axis in two consecutive mocks.

Explain unprompted: replication-lag anomalies, hash vs range partitioning, write skew, fencing tokens, linearizable vs eventual, 2PC vs sagas, log vs queue, exactly-once, LSM vs B-tree, cache stampede, consistent hashing, CDC.
QPS, storage and latency estimates for any familiar product in under a minute; every box in a design has a number next to it.
Nine recorded mocks watched back; each weak axis mapped to a concept and fixed; one external mock with positive feedback on driving the session.
failureModes: Learning without writing. No card = no retention. The card is the deliverable of a concept day, not the reading.
Reading reference designs instead of designing. Design first, compare second, every time.
Skipping the numbers. Hand-wavy estimation is the fastest fail signal in a design round.
Designing silently. Every design is spoken; the round is a conversation, not a drawing.
Never being pushed back on. From week 9 get at least one external mock a week; self-mocks cannot surprise you.
Letting this hour eat the DSA revision block. If a day is short, drop a concept day and do its card on the next recall day.

resources.name: Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann)

concepts.name: Requirements, scoping and the 45-minute framework
master: Turn a vague prompt into three core features and an explicit out-of-scope list in under 4 minutes
Non-functional requirements as numbers: scale, latency per path, consistency vs availability per feature, durability, cost
The order of a round: requirements → numbers → API → data model → high-level diagram → deep dives → trade-offs, with time boxes
Pick the two deep dives yourself before the interviewer does; name the hardest problem in the design out loud
How to take pushback: restate the concern, give the mechanism and its cost, change the design if the concern is right
probes: Which of these features would you drop if you had half the time, and why?
What is the hardest part of this design?
What did you give up to get that?
concepts.read: Hello Interview — 'System Design in a Hurry': Delivery framework + How to approach. Then write your own one-page template.

concepts.name: Back-of-envelope estimation and the numbers card
master: Latency numbers: memory, SSD, disk, same-DC and cross-region round trips; read 1 MB from each
Traffic: DAU × actions → QPS average and 2–3× peak; 1 M/day ≈ 12 QPS; read:write ratio
Storage: row sizes, per-year growth, replication factor, retention; bandwidth in and out
Capacity: what one DB node, one Redis, one Kafka partition, one server of WebSockets handles, by order of magnitude
Cache sizing from the 80/20 rule; when the estimate changes the design (fits in memory? one shard? one region?)
probes: How many QPS is that at peak, and how many machines?
How much storage after five years, with replication?
Does the hot set fit in one Redis?
concepts.read: Jeff Dean's 'Numbers everyone should know' + Hello Interview core concepts: estimation. Then estimate Twitter, YouTube and WhatsApp from memory.

concepts.name: Networking: DNS, TCP/UDP, HTTP, TLS, WebSockets, SSE, long polling
master: DNS resolution and TTL, how DNS is used for load balancing and failover
TCP vs UDP; HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 (multiplexing) vs HTTP/3 (QUIC); where TLS costs latency
WebSockets vs SSE vs long polling: direction, scale limits, proxies, reconnection; when each wins
Latency vs throughput vs bandwidth; head-of-line blocking; keep-alive and connection pooling
probes: Why WebSockets and not SSE for this feature?
What happens to open connections when a server dies?
Where does TLS terminate and why there?
concepts.read: Hello Interview key technologies: networking essentials + realtime updates.

concepts.name: Load balancing, reverse proxies and API gateways
master: L4 vs L7 load balancers; round-robin, least connections, consistent-hash and weighted routing
Health checks, draining, sticky sessions and why to avoid them; global load balancing and anycast
API gateway responsibilities: TLS termination, auth, rate limiting, routing, transformation; the gateway as a bottleneck or single point of failure
Where the load balancer sits in a diagram and what is behind it must be stateless
probes: How does the load balancer know a server is unhealthy?
What breaks if you use sticky sessions?
How would you load-balance WebSockets?
concepts.read: Hello Interview key technologies: load balancers + API gateway.

concepts.name: Scaling patterns and stateless services
master: Vertical vs horizontal scaling and where vertical runs out; scale each tier independently
Stateless services: session state in a store, not in memory; idempotent handlers
The first three bottlenecks every design hits: the database, the hot key, the single coordinator
Capacity planning per component from the numbers; the 10× question and what changes first
probes: What is the first thing to fall over at 10× traffic?
Why must this service be stateless?
How many instances, and how do you know?
concepts.read: Hello Interview core concepts: scaling. Alex Xu vol. 1, ch. 1 (scale from zero to millions).

concepts.name: API design: REST, gRPC, GraphQL, pagination, idempotency, versioning
master: REST resources and verbs; when gRPC (internal, streaming, typed) or GraphQL (client-shaped reads) wins
Pagination: offset vs cursor, and why cursors for feeds; filtering and sorting contracts
Idempotency keys for retried writes; long-running operations (202 + status endpoint)
Versioning and backward compatibility; rate-limit headers; error contracts
probes: How do you make this POST safe to retry?
Why cursor pagination here?
How would clients stay compatible when you change this API?
concepts.read: Hello Interview core concepts: API design. Alex Xu vol. 1 ch. 3 (framework) API section.

concepts.name: Relational databases: indexes, ACID, isolation levels, locking
master: B-tree indexes: composite order, covering indexes, selectivity, index cost on writes
ACID in plain words; isolation levels (read committed, snapshot/repeatable read, serializable) and the anomalies each allows (dirty read, lost update, write skew, phantom)
Optimistic locking (version column, compare-and-set) vs pessimistic (SELECT … FOR UPDATE); when to use each
Where a single relational node tops out and the first scaling moves: read replicas, caching, partitioning
probes: Which isolation level prevents double-booking here, and what does it cost?
Show me the index for this query.
Optimistic or pessimistic locking for this write, and why?
concepts.read: Hello Interview key technologies: databases (SQL). Use the Postgres docs page on transaction isolation for the anomaly table.

concepts.name: NoSQL families and the store decision table
master: Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), document (MongoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j), search (Elasticsearch), time-series: what each buys and costs
Choose by access pattern, join needs, schema change rate, write volume, consistency need — never by fashion
Partition key and sort key thinking in DynamoDB/Cassandra; single-table design
When to say 'Postgres is fine' and when it genuinely is not
probes: Why not just Postgres?
What is the partition key and why?
What query becomes impossible with this store?
concepts.read: Hello Interview key technologies: databases (NoSQL) + DynamoDB/Cassandra pages. Build a one-page decision table.

concepts.name: Storage engines and object storage
master: LSM-trees (memtable, SSTables, compaction, bloom filters) vs B-trees: write vs read amplification, which workload each suits
Write-ahead logs and durability; why Cassandra/RocksDB are write-optimised
Object storage (S3): metadata vs bytes, presigned URLs, multipart and resumable upload, lifecycle tiers, serving via CDN
Blob handling rule: never through your API servers
probes: Why is this store good at writes?
How does a 5 GB upload work end to end?
Where do the bytes live and where does the metadata live?
concepts.read: Hello Interview key technologies: blob storage. A short LSM vs B-tree explainer (e.g. the RocksDB or ScyllaDB blog).

concepts.name: Replication
master: Leader–follower, synchronous vs asynchronous, semi-sync; what each loses on leader failure
Failover: detection, promotion, split-brain, lost writes; RPO and RTO
Replication-lag anomalies and fixes: read-your-writes (route to leader / version check), monotonic reads, consistent prefix
Multi-leader for multi-region or offline clients and the conflict problem; leaderless quorums (N, W, R), hinted handoff
probes: A user posts and does not see their post — why, and how do you fix it?
What happens in the first 30 seconds after the leader dies?
W + R > N: what does that guarantee and what does it not?
concepts.read: Hello Interview core concepts: replication/consistency. Alex Xu vol. 1 ch. 6 (key-value store) replication + quorum sections.

concepts.name: Partitioning, sharding and consistent hashing
master: Hash vs range partitioning; hot spots and skew; shard-key choice is the design
Consistent hashing: ring, virtual nodes, bounded loads; rebalancing without moving everything
Secondary indexes under partitioning: local (scatter-gather) vs global (write cost)
Cross-shard queries and transactions: why to avoid them and what to do when you cannot; resharding live
probes: What is your shard key and what query does it make expensive?
A celebrity's shard is hot — what do you do?
How do you add a node without a thundering migration?
concepts.read: Hello Interview core concepts: sharding + consistent hashing. Alex Xu vol. 1 ch. 5 (consistent hashing).

concepts.name: Consistency models, CAP/PACELC and conflict resolution
master: Linearizable vs causal vs eventual consistency, in one example each; what the user sees
CAP honestly: partition tolerance is not optional; PACELC adds the latency trade-off; which features need which
Conflict resolution: last-write-wins and its data loss, version vectors, merge functions, CRDTs and OT for collaboration
Where strong consistency is actually required: uniqueness, money, inventory, locks
probes: Which parts of this system need strong consistency?
Two users edit at once — what does each see?
What does last-write-wins lose here?
concepts.read: Hello Interview core concepts: consistency + CAP. The Jepsen 'consistency models' map for the vocabulary.

concepts.name: Distributed transactions: 2PC, sagas, outbox, idempotency
master: Two-phase commit: how it works, coordinator failure, why it is avoided at scale
Sagas (choreography vs orchestration) with compensating actions; where partial state is visible
The transactional outbox: write the event with the row, publish from the log; exactly-once effects via idempotent consumers
Idempotency keys and dedup tables; retries that are safe by design
probes: Payment succeeded but the order write failed — what now?
How do you guarantee the event is published if the DB write commits?
What makes this consumer safe under redelivery?
concepts.read: Hello Interview patterns: dealing with contention / sagas. Microservices.io outbox + saga pages.

concepts.name: Data modelling for scale
master: Access-pattern-first modelling: list the queries, then the tables and keys
Denormalisation and when to pay for it; keeping duplicates consistent (events, CDC)
Wide rows, time-bucketed keys, avoiding unbounded partitions; precomputed views for read-heavy paths
Hot-partition avoidance: salting, write sharding, key design for time-series
probes: Show me the schema and the query for the feed.
Why is this partition going to grow without bound?
Which duplicate goes stale first, and how do you fix it?
concepts.read: DynamoDB 'single-table design' guide (Alex DeBrie) + Cassandra data-modelling basics.

concepts.name: Caching strategies
master: Cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-back, write-around: data flow, consistency, failure of each
TTLs, eviction (LRU, LFU), local vs distributed cache, multi-level caches
What to cache (hot, read-heavy, tolerant of staleness) and what never to (money, inventory counts you act on)
Sizing from the numbers; cache hit rate as a design target
probes: What happens on a cache miss storm?
How stale can this value be?
Why write-through here and not cache-aside?
concepts.read: Hello Interview key technologies: Redis + caching patterns. Alex Xu vol. 1 ch. 1 cache section.

concepts.name: Cache problems: invalidation, stampede, hot keys, consistency
master: Invalidation strategies: TTL, event-driven purge, versioned keys; the write-then-invalidate race
Cache stampede / thundering herd: locks, request coalescing, early refresh, jittered TTLs
Hot keys: local caches, key replication, splitting the key; cache cluster resize and consistent hashing
Keeping cache, search index and DB consistent from one change stream
probes: A key expires and 50 k requests hit the DB — what do you do?
How does a write reach the cache?
One key gets 30% of traffic — now what?
concepts.read: Hello Interview patterns: caching deep dives. Facebook's 'Scaling Memcache' paper, sections 3–4 (optional).

concepts.name: CDN and edge delivery
master: Push vs pull CDNs, cache keys, TTLs, invalidation, versioned URLs, origin shielding
What belongs on a CDN (static, media segments, public API responses) and what does not
Edge compute and geo-routing; signed URLs for private content
Cost and cache-hit ratio as first-class design numbers
probes: How do you invalidate a changed image?
What is your CDN hit ratio target and what drives it?
Private video on a CDN — how?
concepts.read: Hello Interview key technologies: CDN. Cloudflare learning centre: what is a CDN.

concepts.name: Real-time delivery and presence
master: Connection servers, routing a message to the right socket (user → server map in Redis / pub/sub)
Presence and heartbeats; last-seen; fan-out of presence changes
Reconnection, backfill since last message id, at-least-once delivery with client dedup
Mobile push (APNs/FCM) as the fallback path; ordering per conversation
probes: User A is on server 3, user B on server 7 — how does the message get there?
The client reconnects after 10 minutes — what does it receive?
How many connections per server and how many servers?
concepts.read: Hello Interview key technologies: realtime updates (WebSockets, pub/sub). Alex Xu vol. 1 ch. 12 (chat system).

concepts.name: Message queues
master: At-most-once vs at-least-once vs exactly-once effects; acknowledgements and visibility timeouts
Dead-letter queues, retries with backoff, poison messages; FIFO queues and ordering limits
Delayed and scheduled delivery; priority; consumer scaling and backlog as a signal
Queue vs log vs database table as a queue: when each is right
probes: What happens if the consumer crashes mid-message?
How do you keep order for one user while scaling consumers?
How deep is the backlog allowed to get?
concepts.read: Hello Interview key technologies: queues (SQS/RabbitMQ). AWS SQS concepts page on visibility timeout and DLQs.

concepts.name: Logs: Kafka, partitions, consumer groups, exactly-once
master: Topics, partitions, partition keys and ordering, replication and ISR
Consumer groups, offsets, rebalancing, consumer lag; retention and compaction
Replaying the log; the log as the source of truth for derived systems
Exactly-once: idempotent producer + transactions, and why idempotent consumers are still needed
probes: How do you guarantee ordering per user?
A consumer is slow — what happens to the others?
Why Kafka here instead of SQS?
concepts.read: Hello Interview key technologies: Kafka. Confluent 'Kafka in 10 minutes' + the exactly-once blog post.

concepts.name: Fan-out patterns
master: Fan-out on write (precomputed inboxes) vs fan-out on read (merge at query time); the celebrity problem and the hybrid
Push vs pull delivery, backlog handling, dedup and ordering of notifications
Rate control and batching; user preferences and quiet hours
Cost model: writes multiplied by followers vs reads multiplied by followees
probes: A user with 50 M followers posts — what happens?
Why precompute the feed and when not to?
How do you avoid sending the same notification twice?
concepts.read: Alex Xu vol. 1 ch. 11 (news feed) + ch. 10 (notification system).

concepts.name: Stream processing and change data capture
master: Windows (tumbling, sliding, session), event time vs processing time, watermarks and late data
Stateful processing, checkpoints, exactly-once semantics in Flink/Kafka Streams
CDC: capture DB changes into a log; keep cache, search and warehouse in sync; event sourcing and CQRS in one paragraph
When stream beats batch and when a nightly job is enough
probes: An event arrives 10 minutes late — which window gets it?
How does the search index learn about a DB update?
What state does this job keep and what happens when it dies?
concepts.read: Hello Interview key technologies: Flink. Debezium 'what is CDC' page.

concepts.name: Batch processing and data pipelines
master: MapReduce / Spark: map, shuffle, reduce; joins and skew; DAG scheduling
Data lake vs warehouse, columnar formats, partitioned tables; idempotent, rerunnable outputs
Lambda vs kappa: batch for correction, stream for freshness; reconciliation jobs
Typical pipelines in interviews: top-K, analytics rollups, index builds, recommendations
probes: How do you recompute yesterday if the job had a bug?
Why both a stream and a batch path?
Where is the skew in this join?
concepts.read: Hello Interview patterns: batch and top-K. Alex Xu vol. 2 ch. (ad click aggregation) batch section.

concepts.name: Failure in distributed systems: partial failure, timeouts, clocks, fencing
master: Partial failure and the three states of a request: succeeded, failed, unknown
Timeouts and unbounded delays; failure detection vs slow nodes; retries make the unknown worse
Clocks lie: time-of-day vs monotonic, skew, why timestamps cannot order writes; leases and process pauses
Fencing tokens: why holding a lock does not prove you still hold it
probes: The request timed out — did it happen?
Two nodes both think they are leader — how, and what protects the data?
Why not order events by timestamp?
concepts.read: Martin Kleppmann's blog post 'How to do distributed locking' (the fencing-token argument). Hello Interview: fault tolerance.

concepts.name: Consensus, coordination, locks and leader election
master: Why consensus exists: leader election, uniqueness, atomic commit; Raft intuition (terms, majority, log replication) in five sentences
ZooKeeper / etcd / Consul: leader election, configuration, service discovery, locks with leases, watches
Distributed locks done right: lease + fencing token; Redlock and its critique
Cost of consensus: latency, availability under partition; keep it off the hot path
probes: How does this system pick a leader and what if it is partitioned?
Where is consensus actually required here?
Why is a Redis lock not enough?
concepts.read: Raft website visualisation (thesecretlivesofdata.com) + etcd 'why etcd' page.

concepts.name: Resilience patterns and rate limiting
master: Timeouts, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, retry budgets; idempotency as the precondition
Circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding, backpressure, graceful degradation
Rate limiting algorithms: token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed/sliding window; distributed limiter with Redis; where it sits; fail-open vs fail-closed
Cascading failures and how retries cause them
probes: Downstream is slow — what does your service do?
Token bucket or sliding window here, and why?
What happens when the rate limiter itself is down?
concepts.read: Hello Interview patterns: rate limiting + resilience. Google SRE book ch. 22 (cascading failures) summary.

concepts.name: Unique IDs, ordering and time
master: UUID v4/v7, Snowflake (timestamp + machine + sequence), ticket servers, DB sequences; sortable IDs and why storage likes them
Clock skew and ID collisions; Lamport timestamps and vector clocks for causality
Ordering guarantees you can and cannot promise across partitions
Sequence numbers per conversation / per stream as the practical answer
probes: How do you generate 100 k unique, roughly sortable IDs per second?
Two datacentres, same millisecond — collision?
How does the client know message order?
concepts.read: Alex Xu vol. 1 ch. 7 (unique ID generator). Twitter Snowflake README.

concepts.name: Multi-region and disaster recovery
master: Active-passive vs active-active; data residency; latency-based routing
Replication across regions and conflict handling; global databases (Spanner, DynamoDB global tables)
Failover drills, RPO/RTO, DNS and traffic shifting; what is not replicated
Cost: replication factor, cross-region bandwidth, operational complexity
probes: A region goes dark — what do users in it experience?
Where can two regions accept writes for the same key?
What is your RPO and how do you know?
concepts.read: Hello Interview patterns: multi-region. AWS 'disaster recovery strategies' whitepaper summary.

concepts.name: Observability, SLOs and operations
master: Logs, metrics, traces; propagate a trace id through queues; what to alert on (symptoms, not causes)
SLIs, SLOs, error budgets; p99 over averages
Capacity planning and autoscaling signals; deploys, rollbacks, feature flags
For every design: what would you monitor, and what is the first alert?
probes: What is the first dashboard you build for this system?
What is the SLO and what happens when you burn the budget?
How do you debug a slow request across six services?
concepts.read: Google SRE book ch. 4 (SLOs) + ch. 6 (monitoring) summaries.

Why a bloom filter here and what is the false-positive cost?
Count unique viewers for a billion events — exactly or approximately?
concepts.read: Alex Xu vol. 2 ch. 1–2 (proximity service, nearby friends). Hello Interview key technologies: geospatial + probabilistic structures.

concepts.name: Media pipelines and payments / ledgers
master: Media: resumable chunked upload, dedup, transcoding DAG, adaptive bitrate (HLS/DASH), thumbnails, CDN, storage tiers

Both: async pipelines with state machines and retries; what is visible to the user while work is pending
Correctness over speed where money is involved; speed over correctness where pixels are

Walk me through a 2 GB video from upload to playback.
How do you prove the books balance?

Microservices vs monolith: boundaries by data ownership, sync vs async coupling, API gateway and service mesh, the distributed-monolith trap

probes: How does service A know the request from B is allowed?
A job runs on two workers at once — how, and how do you stop it?
Why is this a separate service?
